## Clinical trial data is precious {.flip-bg background-image="assets/content-central/AdobeStock_158958915.jpeg" background-size="cover" background-opacity="0.75"}

::: {.absolute top="120" left="60" width="600" style="background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.7); padding: 8px 16px; border-radius: 12px;"}
[*How do a patient's pre-treatment biomarker levels affect the CAR-T therapy manufactured from their T cells?*]{style="font-size: 1.25em"}
:::

::: footer
Stock image
:::

::: {.notes}
- The data I work with is from clinical trials, mostly for cancer treatments
- The patients participating go through grueling treatments, visits that can be hours long, extra procedures that are sometimes painful, sometimes years of follow up visits
- Their time is precious so it's important to get every insight we can from this data for the benefit of these patients and other patients to come
:::


## Clinical data harmonization is tedious & repetitive 

{{< include _manual-workflow-diagram.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
- One way we do this is to do cross-study analysis, combining multiple studies together for additional research to improve on these treatments and look for new ones
- You would think this would be easy, but it's not
- Different subject ID formats, measurement units, date formats, inconsistent categorical values, synonyms for the same laboratory test
- Harmonize, which is just a fancy way to say reformatting from multiple sources to be compatible
- And historically this has been a very complicated and involved process, with lots of manual QC
    - big, complicated diagram
- Many files from many studies, custom code for each input file to output transformation, lots of variation in the code, lots of repeating the same kinds of things over and over again
- Choices of common format might not be the same from harmonization project to harmonization project
- "I'm going to tell you about how I went from this [complicated diagram] to this [simple diagram]"
:::


## Let LLMs do what they're good at

{{< include _llm-workflow-diagram.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
I built out this workflow based on my deep expertise in data harmonization

- match input columns to desired output columns
- figure out what format it's in
- convert it to the format you want it to be
- Overview of some example data from 3 studies (real column names, but not real data)

Data model:

- 🏛️ Columns to include
- 🔑 Primary key(s)
- 📖 Data definition
- 🔢 Data type
- 🏷️ Categorical values
- ❓ Missing value codes
- 📏 Unit of measure

Harmonization configs:

- observed data type, categorical values, missing value codes, units of measure
:::

### Demographics data model

```{.yaml code-line-numbers="1,5,8,14,17|2|3,6,9,15,18|4,7,10,11,16,19,20,21,22"}
unique_subject_id:
  key: true
  data_type: character
  character_pattern: ^[A-Z0-9-]+-\d+-\d+$
site_id:
  data_type: character
  character_pattern: ^\d+$
baseline_height_cm:
  data_type: numeric
  numeric_units: centimeter
  terms:
    loinc: 8302-2
    snomed: C0005890
diagnosis_date:
  data_type: Date
  date_format: "%Y-%m-%d"
actual_arm:
  data_type: factor
  factor_allowed_values:
    - Arm A
    - Arm B
    - Arm C
```

Harmonization configs (input)

- Show example from subjects domain for 3 different studies
- Include baseline height since it will include unit conversion and type conversion
- For each desired output column:
    - Which dataset & column to get it from
    - What data type is it
    - What units is it already in
    - What categorical values exist
- Mention relation to data dictionary? (of recent interest in field)
:::

## Harmonizing a single dataset with modular code + configs

```{.r style="width: 80%; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 1.2em;" code-line-numbers="1,2,3|4-6|7-10"}
harmonize_trial_file <- function(source_file,
                                 config){
  source_df <- read_trial_data_file(source_file)
  harmonized_domain <- source_df |> 
    select(all_of(c(config$model_colname, config$primary_keys))) |> 
    rename(setNames(config$source_colname, config$model_colname)) |> 
    harmonize_data_types(config) |> 
    harmonize_units(config) |> 
    harmonize_missing(config) |> 
    harmonize_factor_values(config)
}
```


## Harmonizing a single dataset with modular code + configs

```{.r style="width: 80%; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 1.2em;" code-line-numbers="1,2|3,4|6-8|9-12"}
harmonize_trial_domain <- function(domain_name,
                                   domain_source_files){
  domain_data_model <- read_data_model(domain_name)
  domain_config <- read_harmonization_config(domain_name)
  
  harmonized_domain_files <- purrr::map(
    domain_source_files,
    \(x) harmonize_trial_file(x, domain_config))
  # Because primary keys are always included, we can
  # use a full_join to combine multiple source files
  harmonized_domain <- purrr::reduce(
    harmonized_domain_files, full_join)
}
```


## Harmonizing all datasets in a trial

```{.r style="width: 80%; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 1.2em;"}
trialX_source_files <- list(
  demographics = c("dm.csv", "adsl.csv"),
  lab_tests = "lb.csv",
  medications = "cm.csv",
  response = "adrs.csv"
)
trialX_harmonized <- purrr::imap(
  trialX_source_files,
  \x(f, d) harmonize_trial_domain(domain = d, domain_source_files = f)
)
```

::: {.notes}
Config-based harmonization code

- Same harmonization code for every domain
- Show code snippets from subjects domain
- Fully working for simple case of just renaming columns and converting data types
- Still to handle (should I mention this or not?):
    - Converting units
    - Harmonizing categorical values
:::


## Much easier to reason about than old code

```{.r .no-scroll-code style="width: 80%; margin: 0 auto; font-size: 1.2em;"}
demographics <- read_csv("adsl.csv") |> 
  select(
    USUBJID, SITE, HEIGHTBL, ACTARM,
    # many more lines of select() ...
  ) |> 
  rename(
    unique_subject_id = USUBJID,
    site_id = SITE,
    baseline_height_cm = HEIGHTBL,
    actual_arm = ACTARM,
    # many more lines of rename() ...
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    baseline_height_cm = in_to_cm(as.numeric(baseline_height_cm)),
    actual_arm = forcats::fct_recode(actual_arm,
      "Arm A: 10M cells" = "Arm A",
      "Arm B: 25M cells" = "Arm B",
      "Standard of care" = "Control"
    )
    # many more lines of mutate()...
  )
```

::: {.notes}
The harmonization config files maximize human attention/time spent reviewing LLM output
- The configs capture the most important parts of the harmonization decisions -- which inputs map to which outputs, and what data transformations happen
- Screenshot of the review app Burak has built
:::

```{=html}
<div style="display: flex; flex-direction: row; align-items: center; justify-content: center; gap: 24px; color: #4F4A4A; font-size: 34px; margin: 30px auto; width: 75%;">
  <div style="display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center; gap: 6px;">
    <div style="padding: 10px 16px; text-align: center; border: 1px solid #000; border-radius: 8px;">Demographics data model</div>
    <div style="font-size: 44px; font-weight: bold;">+</div>
    <div style="padding: 10px 16px; text-align: center; border: 1px solid #000; border-radius: 8px;">Demographics harmonization configs</div>
  </div>
  <div style="font-size: 48px; font-weight: bold;">➡</div>
  <div style="padding: 10px 16px; text-align: center; border: 1px solid #000; border-radius: 8px;">Harmonized demographics data dictionary</div>
</div>
```

:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}

```{.yaml style="margin: 0 auto; font-size: 1.2em;" code-line-numbers="|1-7|3-5|6-7"}
unique_subject_id:
  definition: Unique identifier for each subject across trials
  model: {data_type: character,
          character_pattern: '^[A-Z0-9-]+-\d+-\d+$',
          key: true}
  inputs: [{trial: X, file: adsl.csv, column: USUBJID},
           {trial: Y, file: dm.csv, column: subject_id}]
site_id:
  definition: Study site where the subject was enrolled
  model: {data_type: character,
          character_pattern: '^\d+$'}
  inputs: [{trial: X, file: adsl.csv, column: SITE},
           {trial: Y, file: dm.csv, column: SITE_ID}]
baseline_height_cm:
  definition: Subject height at baseline
  model: {data_type: numeric,
          numeric_units: centimeter,
          terms: {loinc: 8302-2, snomed: C0005890}}
  inputs: [{trial: X, file: adsl.csv, column: HEIGHTBL,
            numeric_units: inch}]
diagnosis_date:
  definition: Date of the subject's initial diagnosis
  model: {data_type: Date,
          date_format: "%Y-%m-%d"}
  inputs: [{trial: X, file: adsl.csv, column: DIAGDTC},
           {trial: Y, file: dm.csv, column: DIAGDTC}]
actual_arm:
  definition: Treatment arm the subject actually received
  model: {data_type: factor,
          factor_allowed_values: [Arm A, Arm B, Arm C]}
  inputs: [{trial: X, file: adsl.csv, column: ACTARM},
           {trial: Y, file: dm.csv, column: study_arm}]
```

:::

::::

::: {.notes}
You get a great data dictionary for your output basically for free with the harmonization configs + data model

- Clear definition of final output data
- Links back to the input dataset + columns that were used
:::

## Takeaways for your own work {.no-title}

::: {style="width: 80%; margin-left:3em;"}
[Be flexible to rapid change]{style="font-size: 2em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.75em; margin-bottom: 0em;"}
[AWS Bedrock agent → langchain agent → Claude Code plugin]{style="font-size: 1em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.5em; margin-bottom: 0em; margin-left: 3em; color: #ADA599;"}

[Design with structured files]{style="font-size: 2em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.75em; margin-bottom: 0em;"}
[.yaml or .json or even .xml]{style="font-size: 1em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.5em; margin-bottom: 0em; margin-left: 3em; color: #ADA599;"}

[Look for data wrangling patterns]{style="font-size: 2em; display: inline-block; margin-top: 0.75em; margin-bottom: 0em;"}
:::

::: {.notes}
- Any project where you're combining data from multiple sources (e.g. COVID data from different health authorities, published datasets from different research groups, eCommerce data from acquired companies, etc.)

- Use data model .yaml to instruct LLM to make the output format you want
- Use a config file that describes all of your inputs (makes it easier for LLM to reason about your data)
- Specification-driven development
- See [`data-dict.yaml`](https://data-dict.tidyverse.org) from Tidyverse

- If you can make it into a function, you make it into a tool call an LLM can use and you can make it reproducible with a structured file
:::
